The Freedman's Savings Bank
Washington, D.C., with branches across the South

Congress chartered a bank for the formerly enslaved, and tens of thousands opened accounts. Its white trustees moved the deposits into risky loans and speculation. When it failed in 1874, many families lost savings they had worked for since freedom.
Always ask whose hands are on your money.
Maggie L. Walker's Penny Savings Bank
Richmond, Virginia

Maggie Lena Walker chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank so Black families could save, borrow and buy homes on fair terms. She was the first woman of any race to charter a bank in the United States.
If they won't lend to you fairly, build the bank.
The Redlining Maps
Every major city, Dayton included
The federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded neighborhoods for lending risk. Black neighborhoods were routinely shaded red, "hazardous," which cut them off from fair mortgages for generations.
The map was drawn on purpose. It can be redrawn on purpose.
The Contract Buyers League
West Side of Chicago

Shut out of mortgages, Black families bought homes "on contract" at inflated prices, losing everything after one missed payment. They organized, withheld payments together and went to court, and forced many sellers to renegotiate.
Read the contract together. Then fight it together.
I AM A MAN
Memphis, Tennessee

Black sanitation workers struck after two co-workers were killed by a faulty truck. Their signs read "I AM A MAN." Dr. King came to Memphis to stand with them. The strike won union recognition and a raise.
Dignity is a wage demand.
The Montgomery Bus Boycott
Montgomery, Alabama
For 381 days, Black riders walked, carpooled and organized rather than ride segregated buses. The lost fares hurt the bus company, and the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation.
Your money is a vote. Spend it like one.
The People's Free Medical Clinics
Late 1960s–1970s
Oakland and cities nationwide
The Black Panther Party opened free community clinics and ran a national screening campaign for sickle cell anemia, a disease the medical system had long neglected.
When care won't come to the block, the block brings care.
Dr. Charles Drew
New York and Washington, D.C.
Dr. Drew pioneered ways to store blood plasma and ran a major wartime blood-bank program. He spoke out against the Red Cross separating donated blood by race.
Expertise is protection. Learn the system better than it knows you.
Wilberforce University
founded 1856
Wilberforce, Ohio (next to Xenia)
In 1863 the AME Church bought Wilberforce, making it the first college owned and operated by African Americans. Central State University grew up beside it. Both are minutes from Dayton.
We have always built our own schools.
Dunbar, the Wrights and the Dayton Tattler
West Third Street, Dayton
Paul Laurence Dunbar and Orville Wright were classmates at Dayton's Central High School. In 1890 the Wright brothers printed Dunbar's newspaper for Dayton's Black community, the Dayton Tattler.
The block reads, and the block writes its own story.
Mayor James H. McGee
Dayton, Ohio
Dayton elected James H. McGee its first Black mayor. He served for twelve years, and a West Dayton boulevard carries his name.
Get a voice in the room where the rules are written.
Greenwood: Black Wall Street
Tulsa, Oklahoma
Greenwood was a thriving Black business district of banks, theaters and shops. A white mob destroyed it in the 1921 massacre. Residents rebuilt much of it within years, with little help.
What we build can be taken. What we know can't.
